covers.quote: The word ‘disinterested’ means ‘impartial’ and ‘unbiased by personal interest’.
The word ‘uninterested’ means ‘not interested’, ‘indifferent’ or ‘unconcerned’.

parts.quote: The judge’s deliberation was disinterested and considered.
The invitation to the concert was wasted on me because I’m uninterested in jazz music.

rules.quote: ‘Disinterested’ is often used to mean ‘uninterested’, but this use is not correct.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Disinterested’ is used to mean not interested, indifferent or unconcerned.
when: When ‘disinterested’ expresses a lack of interest rather than impartiality.
rules.why: The explicit rejection of this usage is actionable; the surrounding definitions explain the distinction rather than create additional rules.

covers.quote: The word ‘dove’ is the past tense of ‘dive’ in American English.

parts.quote: Bystanders dived into the creek to help the drowning swimmer.

rules.quote: In Australian English, write ‘dived’ to use the past tense of the verb ‘to dive’.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Dove’ is used as the past tense of ‘dive’ in Australian English.
when: When writing the past tense of ‘dive’ in Australian English.
rules.why: G-2: the Australian-English and verb-tense conditions belong to one spelling check.

covers.quote: for all intents and purposes/for all intensive purposes

parts.quote: The paperwork may take a few weeks to come through but, for all intents and purposes, you are hired.

rules.quote: The correct expression is ‘for all intents and purposes’, meaning ‘in every practical sense’.
rules.violation_condition: The expression is written as ‘for all intensive purposes’.
when: When using the expression meaning ‘in every practical sense’.
rules.why: G-4: the body states the correct expression; the heading supplies the contrasting incorrect form.

covers.quote: The exception is a court decision; write this as ‘judgment’.

parts.quote: You can speak to one of our counsellors without fearing judgement.
Please cite the High Court’s most recent judgment in the issues paper.

rules.violation_condition: ‘Judgment’ is used for a non-court sense, or ‘judgement’ is used for a court decision.
when: Use ‘judgement’ for senses other than a court decision.
Use ‘judgment’ for a court decision.
rules.why: G-2: the court-decision exception changes which spelling is required, not the identity of the check.

parts.quote: The chemical symbol for lead is ‘Pb‘.

rules.quote: ‘Lead’ (not led) means a base metal and is pronounced as ‘led’.
rules.violation_condition: The name of the base metal is written ‘led’ instead of ‘lead’.
when: When referring to the base metal.
rules.why: The explicit ‘not led’ correction supports a spelling check for the metal; it does not turn the other definitions in this section into rules.

covers.quote: master degree/masters degree/master’s degree
When referring to a specific qualification, use ‘Master of [area of study]’.

parts.quote: He completed his master degree last year.
Having a Master of Arts helped her gain the promotion.
The university offered several master degrees to postgraduate students.

rules.violation_condition: A generic master-level degree is called ‘masters degree’ or ‘master’s degree’, including plural degree forms, or a specific qualification is named in a form other than ‘Master of [area of study]’.
when: For a generic reference, use ‘master degree’ or its plural ‘master degrees’.
When referring to a specific qualification, use ‘Master of [area of study]’.
rules.why: G-2: generic degree references and specific qualification names are conditional forms of the same naming check.

covers.quote: Use ‘program’ for the titles of new programs based on government policy.
Use ‘programme’ only when it is part of the formal name of an existing program.

parts.quote: One of the most challenging aspects of our work is designing programs that can be implemented quickly.
The Prescription Shopping Programme lets medical practitioners check their patients’ prescription histories.

rules.quote: Use ‘program’ rather than ‘programme’, including for computer programs.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Programme’ is used other than as part of the formal name of an existing program.
when: Includes computer programs.
Includes titles of new programs based on government policy.
‘Programme’ is allowed when it is part of the formal name of an existing program.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: computer programs, new titles and existing formal names are cases of one spelling rule, not separate findings.

covers.quote: ‘Irregardless’ is likely a combination of the words ‘irrespective’ and ‘regardless’. It is not accepted as standard Australian English.

parts.quote: Our aim is for all staff to have access to this training, regardless of location.
The following instructions will work regardless of which mobile platform you use.
These are interesting times but we must carry on regardless.

when: When choosing between ‘regardless’ and ‘irregardless’.
rules.why: G-4: the instruction and the rejection of ‘irregardless’ describe one word-choice check.

covers.quote: ‘Would of’ is incorrect.

parts.quote: If I had known we were over budget, I would have changed the scope of the contract.
This would’ve spared us a lot of stress
At the very least, we would of avoided the overspend.

rules.quote: Always write ‘would have’ or the contracted form ‘would’ve’.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Would of’ is used as the verb form ‘would have’.
when: When expressing the verb form ‘would have’; the contraction ‘would’ve’ is also correct.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the full and contracted forms are alternatives within one check; the rejection of ‘would of’ restates it.
